understanding.purpose: एक ही ग्रह के नामों को तीन भारतीय लिपियों में दिखाना और उसकी सूर्य से दूरी तथा टिप्पणी देना।
understanding.reading: पाठक प्रत्येक पंक्ति में ग्रह के नामों का मिलान करेगा, फिर दूरी और टिप्पणी पढ़ेगा; वह ग्रहों के बीच दूरियों की तुलना भी कर सकता है।
groups: स्तंभ 1–3 एक ही ग्रह के नाम हैं; इन्हें साथ और इतना चौड़ा रखना चाहिए कि नाम पहचानने योग्य रहें।
स्तंभ 4–5 ग्रह के गुण बताते हैं: दूरी संक्षिप्त तुलनीय संख्या है, जबकि टिप्पणी विस्तृत वर्णन है।
keep_intact: तीनों लिपियों में ग्रहों के नाम
दूरी के दशमलव मान और AU इकाई
जहाँ संभव हो, टिप्पणी के शब्द
may_wrap: टिप्पणियाँ शब्दों के बीच कई पंक्तियों में आ सकती हैं; उनकी लंबाई से बनने वाली पंक्ति की ऊँचाई दूसरे कक्षों में भी समा सकती है।
दूरी का शीर्षक शब्द और इकाई के बीच दो पंक्तियों में आ सकता है।

bad.why: The narrow notes column splits words and produces an eight-line cell, making the last row disproportionately tall and difficult to scan. The distance header also wraps.

final.rationale: r3C keeps the three planet-name columns compact, the distance header on one line, and the notes free of mid-word splits. Its wider notes column gives the first data row a more manageable height than r2C, while requiring slightly less horizontal scrolling than r3A. The names and distances remain visible in the initial viewport, though readers must scroll to read the ends of notes.

general: Protect intact words and identifiers when breaking them would make a table harder to read.
Allocate width according to content and column roles; long prose often benefits more from extra width than short labels or numbers.
Judge horizontal scrolling against the readability and row height gained by allowing it.
specific: The first three columns identify the same planets in different scripts, so each needs enough width for its own longest name.
The notes column contains much longer multilingual text than the other columns and drives most of the table's height.
Keeping the distance header on one line preserves a compact header while its values remain visible before scrolling.

final.tradeoffs: r3B requires only 33px of horizontal scrolling, but wraps the distance header and makes the last row taller. r3A gives the notes more space than r3C at the cost of another 15px of scrolling.
final.uncertain: A designer prioritizing minimal scrolling could reasonably prefer r3B or r1B. The ranges are approximate, untested width tolerances around r3C; line breaks and row heights may change within them.

A.why: The whole table fits in the viewport and the planet names remain intact, but the narrow comments column produces many short lines and splits Tamil words.

B.why: The planet names and distance header read comfortably, and the wider comments column reduces wrapping. The comments extend beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to read them.

C.why: The comments are squeezed into a very narrow strip, creating excessive wrapping and word splits. Tamil planet names also break across lines, making rows harder to scan.

D.why: The planet names remain intact and the comments have more room than in A. Some comment text lies beyond the viewport, and the distance header wraps.

E.why: The unwrapped distance header and wider comments give the table a clear rhythm, though readers must scroll sideways to finish reading the comments.

F.why: The planet names stay intact and the comments are less cramped than in A. The wrapped distance header and off-screen comment text make scanning slightly less convenient.

reviews.unsure: The right edges of the wider layouts extend beyond the supplied image, so their full widths and the complete wrapping of their comments cannot be judged precisely.

A.why: The wide first two columns leave the comment column extremely narrow. Frequent word splits and very tall rows make comparisons difficult.

B.why: The planet names and distance header remain intact, and the wider comment column gives the rows a readable rhythm. Much of the comment column requires horizontal scrolling.

C.why: The whole table fits in the viewport and the planet names remain intact, but the narrow comment column splits long words and makes the last row very tall.

D.why: The generous comment column reduces wrapping while keeping names and the distance header intact. The reader must scroll horizontally to read the full comments.

E.why: The columns for names are compact and the comments have more room than in C. Some comment text lies beyond the viewport, and the distance header wraps.

F.why: The compact name columns leave useful space for comments, with only modest horizontal scrolling. The distance header wraps, and the longest comment still takes several lines.

reviews.unsure: The screenshots do not show the full right edge of every wider layout, so the total scrolling distance and whether every long comment remains intact are difficult to judge precisely.
